coach_says: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count who attacks the square. After d4 the pawn on d4 is hit three times (the e5 pawn, the Nc6 and the Bb6 aiming down the a7-g1 diagonal) and defended only twice (Nf3, Qd1), so after Nxd4 you simply lose a pawn. A quiet d3 keeps everything solid; prepare d4 later with c3 or Re1 if you want it.

You missed a free pawn: Bxd4! wins the d4 pawn because its main defender, the e3 pawn, can't really recapture. If exd4, the e-file opens and Rxe1+ Qxe1 Qxd4+ wins the pawn back with check and hits the Bc4 too. Whenever a defender sits in front of a piece on an open file, ask whether it is really free to capture. b6 is a slow move that gives that chance away.
concept: d4 pawn defended by a pinned pawn

coach_says: Castling put your king on g1, a knight's jump from e2, with your queen on g3 also a knight's jump away: Ne2+ forks king and queen. Before castling, check what enemy pieces can reach the squares around your new king; the Nd4 was already eyeing c2, e2 and f3. Nc3 was the move, covering e2 and e4 and developing a piece.

Your knight on e6 was the only piece guarding g7, which White's queen on f7 and bishop on d4 were both aiming at. Taking on g5 pulled that guard away and Bxg7 is checkmate, since your own h7 pawn takes the king's escape square. When the opponent has two pieces lined up on a square next to your king, the piece defending it must stay put.

White's e4 pawn had no defender at all, so Nxe4 won a central pawn straight away. After exd4 White gets to play e5, kicking your knight from f6 with tempo and the e4 pawn is no longer there to take. When the opponent leaves a pawn loose, take it before making an exchange that gives them a useful move.

Your queen was attacked and you had two captures: Qxa5 trades queens, then Rxd7 wins the pawn back with your rook on the seventh, a rook endgame a pawn down that is usually a draw. Qxd7 keeps queens on, and after Re1+ the rooks come off, leaving a queen endgame where Black's passed b-pawn and checks against your king are very hard to defend. When you are behind, look for the trade that leads to the most drawish ending.
concept: trade queens to reach rook ending
also: outside passed pawn in queen endings

coach_says: Black's big threat was Nd4, hitting your queen on f3 and the c2 pawn (Nxc2+ would fork your king and rook). Nh3 does nothing about it and puts the knight on the edge, so after Nd4 your queen has to run and c2 falls or you lose more. c3 takes the d4 square away from the knight. Each move, ask what the opponent wants to do next, especially with a knight near your queen.

Your e4 pawn was attacked by the Nf6 and nothing defended it, so after cxd4 Black just takes it with Nxe4. e5 first solves that with tempo: it hits the knight on f6 and the bishop on d6, Black has to deal with it (Re8 pinning the pawn), and you take back on d4 next move with your pawn safe. Before recapturing, check whether a piece or pawn of yours is left hanging.

Re7 does guard against Bxf7+, which was a real threat, but you had something better: Rxe3. The e3 pawn was attacked by your rook and your queen on g5 and defended only by the Re2, so if Rxe3 then Qxe3+ comes with check, and Bxf7+ no longer wins anything. Count attackers and defenders on weak pawns, and look for captures before defending.
concept: e3 pawn attacked twice, defended once

coach_says: White was threatening bxc5 bxc5 Nxd4: if you take back with the pawn, Qxd4 hits your rook on h8 and bishop on d6 at once, because the d4 pawn was all that blocked the long diagonal. f5 does nothing about that and opens the e8-h5 diagonal, so Qh5+ forces your king to walk and you can never castle. Nbc6, adding a defender to d4, or Qc8 offering a queen trade, kept you in the game.

Your a2 pawn was attacked by the rook on a8, so Qxb6 only swaps your a-pawn for the b6 pawn, and after Rxa2 Black's rook sits on your second rank hitting b2 and c2. Before grabbing a pawn, check what you are leaving hanging. a3 kept the pawn and the rook out, and you could think about b6 later.
concept: rook gets to your second rank

coach_says: Ra5 is fine: it moves your rook with tempo, attacking the queen on d5. Rc4 or Re6 were about as good. You are worse because of the earlier lost pawn, not because of this move.
Ne5 is a good move: the knight lands on a strong central square, eyes f7 and d7, and supports your attack against Black's loose king. d5 was equally strong. Keep going like this.
2.Bc4 is a perfectly sound opening move, the Bishop's Opening, aiming at f7. Nf3 is more common, but there is nothing to correct here.

The position was already lost: your bishop on c5 was hanging to the Re5 and your king is exposed. Kd6 defends the bishop but walks into Rd5+, and the rook then takes on c5; Be7 saving the bishop was a little better. Watch for checks when you defend a piece with your king, but the damage was done earlier.
also: defending with the king invites checks

coach_says: Qb3 is fine: it protects the c2 pawn your rook on c8 was eyeing and puts pressure on d5. Qd3 was about the same. You are a pawn down, but this move doesn't make it worse.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a sound and solid reply to 1.e4. It is just as good as 1...e5; nothing to fix.

You are up a lot, but your king had no escape square: the rook on f1 blocks it, and Black's rook on h8 covers h2. So after a5, Bh2+ Kh1 and the bishop can give discovered checks from the h-file forever, a draw by perpetual check. Ra1 (or any rook move off f1, or g3) frees f1 for your king first, then the a-pawn can run. When winning, look at your king's safety before pushing pawns.
also: give your king an escape square

coach_says: Qg7+ looks active, but Rg2 blocks the check and pins your queen to your king on the g-file, with White's queen on h6 also attacking g7, so you lose your queen for a rook. Before giving a check, look at how the opponent can block it and whether the blocking piece then attacks you. Qxe5, taking a free central pawn, was the right move.
concept: check that walks into a pin

coach_says: Your b4 pawn was blocking the diagonal from Black's queen on d6 to your knight on a3. When it captured on a5 it opened that line, and Qxa3 wins the undefended knight, then the a5 pawn too. When a pawn or piece moves, check what it was shielding. Nxb5, saving the knight with an attack on the queen and keeping the threat of bxa5, was better.
concept: opened a line to your loose knight
